canonical_statement: The study evaluated alternative strategies for defining an UFH therapeutic range and their effects on therapeutic classification when changing aPTT reagents.
Sample set 1 comprised 39 anonymized sodium-citrate samples from adult patients receiving UFH at either of two hospitals over 3 months.

population.label: 39 anonymized sodium-citrate samples from adults receiving UFH at hospital A or B

canonical_statement: Sample set 1 included adults receiving UFH regardless of possible concomitant anticoagulants such as vitamin K antagonists.

population.label: Adults receiving UFH; concomitant anticoagulants permitted

canonical_statement: Sample-set-1 specimens were centrifuged within 30 minutes, plasma stored at -20 C, then thawed and analyzed simultaneously in both laboratories.
aPTT was measured by mechanical clot detection on STA-R; hospital A used STA and Cephascreen reagents, while hospital B used Cephascreen from a different batch.
Both hospitals measured anti-Xa activity with STA Liquid Anti-Xa calibrated by MultiHep without exogenous antithrombin; anti-Xa was successfully measured in 32 of 39 sample-set-1 specimens.
Sample set 2 comprised 70 serial samples from 8 UFH-treated patients at hospital A collected over 4 months.

population.label: 70 serial samples from 8 UFH-treated patients at hospital A

canonical_statement: Sample set 2 used the same analytical conditions as sample set 1 except measurement within 6 hours of blood draw and a different Cephascreen reagent lot.
Protocol A derived the Cephascreen aPTT range by linear regression against anti-Xa activity and used aPTT values corresponding to 0.3-0.7 U/mL anti-Xa.
Protocol B directly used 0.3-0.7 U/mL anti-Xa activity as the UFH therapeutic range.
Protocol C defined the Cephascreen aPTT therapeutic range as 1.5-2.5 times the reagent upper reference limit.
Protocol D applied hospital B's existing Cephascreen aPTT therapeutic range to hospital A results.

Laboratory comparisons used linear regression and R-squared; within-patient variation used the quartile coefficient of dispersion, and its relation to body weight used second-degree polynomial regression.
In sample set 1, Cephascreen aPTT correlated poorly with anti-Xa activity (R2=0.2686).

canonical_statement: Using consecutive samples from a small number of individual patients could introduce patient-related bias into aPTT/anti-Xa correlations.
The study did not measure antithrombin levels, so the proposed explanation of low anti-Xa activity during prolonged UFH therapy as acquired antithrombin deficiency was not tested.
Sample-set-2 specimens could be analyzed up to 6 hours after centrifugation, whereas the authors cite a 4-hour CLSI interval as optimal.
The study did not evaluate clinical bleeding or thrombotic outcomes resulting from the different therapeutic-range strategies.
Between-method, between-batch, and between-laboratory variation in both aPTT and anti-Xa assays likely impedes standardized definition of an UFH therapeutic range.
The authors concluded that different therapeutic-range strategies can produce clinically relevant differences in projected UFH dosing and should be critically evaluated.
When an aPTT reagent is changed, the authors advise thorough validation of the adapted UFH nomogram to identify effects on therapeutic classification.
